target_identification.speaker: Jane
target_identification.anchor_quote:
There is no dishonour, no breach of promise, no desertion in the case.
I am not under the slightest obligation to go to India, especially with
strangers. With you I would have ventured much, because I admire,
confide in, and, as a sister, I love you; but I am convinced that, go
when and with whom I would, I should not live long in that climate.

T.reason: Jane directly avows love as an emotional and relational state. The qualification “as a sister” specifies that the love is familial rather than romantic but does not weaken its clear truth-presenting form.

evidence.quotation: as a sister, I love you

P.reason: The focal avowal does not undertake marriage, travel, missionary service, or another obligation. Jane expressly denies being bound to go to India. Her separate offer to serve as St John’s assistant and her statement that she “would have ventured much” explain what her sisterly affection had made conceivable; they do not turn “I love you” into a commitment. St John has also rejected the assistant-only arrangement, so there is no uptake of it as their agreed bond.

E.reason: This is a controlled, explanatory avowal embedded in Jane’s reasoned rebuttal of an alleged obligation. It is not represented as a reflexive cry or affective discharge.

O.reason: Beyond avowing affection, the expression helps define and limit the relationship: Jane classifies her love as sisterly, thereby distinguishing it from the marital love St John seeks and explaining why trust in him does not entail marriage or an obligation to travel.

I say again, I will be your

original_speech_situation: Jane is resisting St John’s claim that she has promised or engaged herself to missionary work in India. She says that her admiration, trust, and sisterly love made her willing to venture much with him, while denying any obligation to go with strangers and maintaining her refusal to become his wife.
undertaking_and_uptake: The focal expression avows and qualifies affection but creates no undertaking. Jane’s assistant-only offer is a separate act, and St John rejects that arrangement as unsuitable; she explicitly denies any promise or obligation to go to India. The avowal’s sisterly framing also excludes uptake as acceptance of his marriage proposal.
recognition_note: I recognize the supplied passage as from Charlotte Brontë’s Jane Eyre. The classification uses only the supplied blocks and reference metadata.
limitations: The supplied evidence strongly establishes the avowal’s sisterly, non-marital force in this exchange. It cannot by itself settle every aspect of Jane’s longer-term intentions or the future course of the relationship.
